title: Percussion added to jazz groups
summary: Conga players add little in straight 4/4 jazz and Chico agrees.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: Yeah. I noticed that, when you get -- when they were kind of doing what was not really Afro-Cuban jazz, what kind of jazz Afro-Cuban (inaudible) is, you know, like add a conga or add a bongo to a regular group, and they're using the 4/4 beat, just get -- it -- the Latin percussionist sounds like a fifth wheel, because he's just able to go chica-chica, chica.

I don't like it. You know why? In many places they (inaudible) to be there. (Inaudible) Chico talking about seems like a Chico (inaudible). The last night he go through here, downtown when the -- in the college downtown and was one particular number, and Chico said, you see, that's what I dislike. That conga player ain't got no business to be there. What is for him to be playing there? Don't mean nothing. In fact, he's in somebody's way, don't add nothing to the thing and conflict because the drummer playing one thing, and what he play, boom-boom, boom-boom, like somebody playing the mariachas, don't mean nothing. I know it don't mean nothing.
IF YOU DON'T PLAY THAT WAY
If you can play straight jazz (inaudible) the drum, ain't got no business to have that thing in there.

I noticed there was some recording (inaudible) recently with Parker's regular group, with Teddy Kotik and people, later group and the, I think, Manguale and Miranda, I think. Anyway, it comes out in bongo. And most
of those numbers have that problem, because they -- the -- the percussionists, they're limited because there's no clave field. You don't get that spreading over two bars.
